entries.text: Columbia Masterworks ML 5060 — the June 1955 sessions at 30th Street, issued early 1956 — is still the recording that made the piano Goldberg a public fact. About thirty-eight minutes, no repeats, contrapuntal lines cut with a clarity that was then almost theatrical. Against Schiff’s near-complete-repeats Decca of 1982 it is a different work: a debut document rather than a cycle that unfolds in three large arcs. Against Gould’s own 1981 remake it is the hotter, leaner object — the one the National Recording Registry inducted in 2003. Later Gould disliked some of its tempi and the nocturne-like Variation 25; that self-criticism does not retire the disc. For a first piano Goldberg in the house, this remains the Référence: the performance that opened the door, not the one that closed the argument.

CBS Masterworks Digital IM 37779 — April–May 1981 at the same 30th Street studio, issued September 1982 — is not a remaster of 1955. Selected first-half repeats, roughly fifty-one minutes, a late architecture built around canons and four-part writing rather than debut bravura. It took the 1983 Grammy for Best Classical Album and a Diapason d’Or (n° 278, December 1982). Beside the 1955 Référence it is the deeper second thought; beside Schiff’s Decca it is still Gould’s instrument and Gould’s edit, not a complete-repeats survey. Keep both Goulds if you can. If the shelf has room for only one late-studio piano Goldberg with selective repeats and digital-era presence, this is the disc — without displacing 1955 as the landmark.

Decca 417 116-2 — Kingsway Hall, 13–15 April 1982, producer Michael Haas, engineer Simon Eadon — is Schiff’s first studio Goldberg, not the ECM Basel live remake of 2001. Near-complete repeats (Aria da capo excepted), about seventy-two minutes, conceived in three large sections; some repeats taken an octave up or down, a habit Distler notes he later dropped. Against Gould 1955 it restores duration and symmetry the mono debut refused; against Gould 1981 it is another pianist’s complete-repeats world, warmer and less canonic in obsession. Two stars: a serious Decca piano alternative that belongs on the assessed shelf, not a third Gould. Do not confuse the April 1982 tapes with December 1982 Kingsway couplings on neighbouring Decca faces.
